equation.name: How strongly one gas molecule scatters light
equation.formula:
n = 1 + max(n1, 0)
a = (n * n - 1) / (n * n + 2)
l2 = lambda * lambda
sigma = 24 * pi * pi * pi * a * a / (l2 * l2 * N * N) * F

n1.name: how much the gas bends light (n − 1)

N.name: number density the refractivity was measured at

source.text: Bodhaine, B. A., Wood, N. B., Dutton, E. G. and Slusser, J. R. 1999, On Rayleigh optical depth calculations, J. Atmos. Oceanic Technol. 16, 1854

explain.curious: Air molecules scatter blue light far more than red, as the inverse fourth power of wavelength: that is why the sky is blue and sunsets red.
explain.science: Rayleigh scattering by molecules much smaller than the wavelength, from the gas's refractive index (Lorentz-Lorenz) with the King factor for non-spherical molecules.

equation.name: How much dry air bends light of each colour
equation.formula:
s2 = 1 / (lambda * per_um * lambda * per_um)
n1 = (A + B / (C - s2) + Dd / (E - s2)) * scale

scale.name: the fit gives (n − 1) in units of 10⁻⁸

n1.name: how much dry air bends light (n − 1)

source.text: Peck, E. R. and Reeder, K. 1972, Dispersion of air, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 62, 958

explain.curious: Air bends light by about three parts in ten thousand, a little more for blue than red.
explain.science: Measured dispersion of dry air at 15 °C and one atmosphere, 230 nm to 1.7 µm.

explain.curious: Looking straight up from Earth's surface, about one in ten blue-green photons is scattered on the way through; Venus's air scatters almost all of them.
explain.science: The column above the surface holds P / (m̄ g) molecules per unit area, each scattering with cross-section σ. Bodhaine et al. evaluate g at the column's mass-weighted height; this block takes g as given.
